result.topic_en: Starting from the q-binomial theorem, the page proves a finite identity for the product (c-1)(c-x)...(c-x^{n-1}) and an expansion of c^n, then uses them to find the coefficient of a^n in a series of ratios of infinite products; it is pencil-annotated "Rogers-R fuln" (Rogers–Ramanujan functions).
result.transcription:
Add MS a 94 18 (18) (18)

Assuming $\frac{\Pi(b,x)}{\Pi(-a,x)} = 1 + \frac{a+b}{1-x} + \frac{(a+b)(a+bx)}{(1-x)(1-x^2)} + \cdots$

it can be proved that

(1) $(c-1)(c-x)(c-x^2)\cdots\cdots(c-x^{n-1})$

$= c^n - c^{n-1}\frac{1-x^n}{1-x} + c^{n-2}x\cdot\frac{(1-x^n)(1-x^{n-1})}{(1-x)(1-x^2)} - c^{n-3}x^3\cdot\frac{(1-x^n)(1-x^{n-1})(1-x^{n-2})}{(1-x)(1-x^2)(1-x^3)}$

$+ \cdots\cdots$

n being any positive integer

(2). $c^n = 1 + (c-1)\frac{1-x^n}{1-x} + (c-1)(c-x)\frac{(1-x^n)(1-x^{n-1})}{(1-x)(1-x^2)} +$

$(c-1)(c-x)(c-x^2)\cdot\frac{(1-x^n)(1-x^{n-1})(1-x^{n-2})}{(1-x)(1-x^2)(1-x^3)} + \cdots$

for the coeff^t. of $c^n$ is 1 and all other coeffts. can be shewn to be 0 by taking the coefft. of $c^r$ and applying the result (1).

(3). Now the coeff^t. of $a^n$ in

$\frac{\Pi(-a,x)}{\Pi(-ab,x)} + a\cdot\frac{(1-b)(1-c)}{1-x}\cdot\frac{\Pi(-ax,x)}{\Pi(-ab,x)} +$

$a^2\cdot\frac{(1-b)(x-b)(1-c)(x-c)}{(1-x)(1-x^2)}\cdot\frac{\Pi(-ax^2,x)}{\Pi(-ab,x)} + \cdots$

$= \frac{(b-1)(b-x)\cdots(b-x^{n-1})}{(1-x)(1-x^2)\cdots(1-x^n)} + \frac{(1-b)(1-c)}{1-x}\cdot\frac{(b-x)(b-x^2)\cdots(b-x^{n-1})}{(1-x)(1-x^2)\cdots(1-x^{n-1})}$

$+ \frac{(1-b)(x-b)(1-c)(x-c)}{(1-x)(1-x^2)}\cdot\frac{(b-x)(b-x^2)\cdots(b-x^{n-2})\{+(b-x^{n-1})+\}}{(1-x)(1-x^2)\cdots[-(1-x^{n-2})-]} + \cdots$

$= \frac{(b-1)(b-x)\cdots(b-x^{n-1})}{(1-x)(1-x^2)\cdots(1-x^n)}\left\{1 + (c-1)\cdot\frac{1-x^n}{1-x} + (c-1)(c-x)\cdot\frac{(1-x^n)(1-x^{n-1})}{(1-x)(1-x^2)} + \cdots\right\}$

[pencil, circled:] Rogers-R fuln
